marrow__ANAT_CH42_Q001.takeaway: Intercostal nerves are ventral rami of thoracic spinal nerves; T7–T11 continue onto abdominal wall and T12 forms subcostal nerve.
marrow__ANAT_CH42_Q001.displayText: The intercostal nerve is a branch of the ventral (anterior) ramus of a thoracic spinal nerve. The source notes that intercostal nerves are distributed primarily to the thoracic and abdominal walls: the first thoracic nerve contributes variably to the second nerve and passes into the brachial plexus; T3-T6 supply only the thoracic wall; T7-T11 supply both thoracic and abdominal walls; and the subcostal nerve supplies the abdominal wall and gluteal skin. Lateral and anterior cutaneous branches innervate the anterior chest wall, and the source identifies T6 with the xiphoid process.

rationales.b: Dorsal thoracic rami also supply back structures rather than the intercostal spaces.
rationales.d: Cervical ventral rami contribute to cervical plexus and brachial plexus, not intercostal nerves.

marrow__ANAT_CH42_Q003.takeaway: Intercostal nerves run between internal and innermost intercostals, not between external and internal layers; the latter statement is the false one.
marrow__ANAT_CH42_Q003.displayText: The marked structure is the intercostal nerve. The false statement is that intercostal nerves lie between the external and internal intercostal muscles; the source places them between the internal and innermost intercostal muscles. Typical intercostal nerves supply only the thoracic wall, with the source describing T3-T6 as typical; upper intercostal nerves have special distributions, T2 gives the intercostobrachial nerve, and T7-T11 continue to the abdominal wall as thoracoabdominal nerves. In each intercostal space the main neurovascular bundle is arranged superior-to-inferior as vein, artery, nerve (VAN), with a collateral SVAN bundle.

marrow__ANAT_CH42_Q005.takeaway: The intercostobrachial nerve is the lateral cutaneous branch of T2 and supplies axilla and upper medial arm.
marrow__ANAT_CH42_Q005.displayText: The clinical picture suggests injury to the intercostobrachial nerve, which is a branch of the second intercostal nerve. It is the lateral cutaneous branch of T2 and supplies skin of the axilla and upper medial arm. The source highlights its vulnerability during mastectomy, axillary nerve blocks and other axillary surgeries, and identifies it as a source of referred cardiac pain.

marrow__ANAT_CH42_Q006.takeaway: A mid-axillary chest tube passes through intercostal muscle layers; transversus thoracis is anterior and is not pierced at this site.
marrow__ANAT_CH42_Q006.displayText: Intercostal drainage tubes are placed in the mid-axillary line, and transversus thoracis is not pierced because it lies anteriorly rather than in the mid-axillary line. The source also calls transversus thoracis triangularis sternae or sternocostalis, gives its origin from the lower third of the posterior surface of the sternum, xiphoid process and lower 3-4 rib cartilages, and its insertion into cartilages of the second to sixth ribs. The innermost muscle plane includes innermost intercostals laterally, subcostals posteriorly and transversus thoracis anteriorly.

marrow__ANAT_CH42_Q007.takeaway: Phrenic nerve carries sensory fibers from diaphragmatic parietal peritoneum as well as motor supply to the hemidiaphragm.
marrow__ANAT_CH42_Q007.displayText: The left phrenic nerve supplies sensory fibers to the parietal peritoneum covering the diaphragm. The source states that it is a mixed nerve derived mainly from C4 with contributions from C3 and C5 ventral rami, formed at the lateral border of scalenus anterior. It descends anterior to the pulmonary hilum between mediastinal pleura and fibrous pericardium, passes through the muscular diaphragm just anterior to the central tendon, and supplies motor fibers to the ipsilateral hemidiaphragm plus sensory fibers to mediastinal pleura, fibrous/serous pericardium and diaphragmatic peritoneum.

rationales.a: Phrenic nerve arises from ventral rami C3–C5, chiefly C4, not dorsal rami C2–C4.
rationales.b: It descends between mediastinal pleura and fibrous pericardium, not freely within pleural space.
rationales.d: The left phrenic passes through muscular diaphragm anterior to central tendon, not the vena caval opening.

marrow__ANAT_CH42_Q008.takeaway: Pericardial somatic afferents travel in the phrenic nerve and can refer pain to C3–C5 shoulder/neck dermatomes.
marrow__ANAT_CH42_Q008.displayText: The pain of pericarditis is carried by the phrenic nerve. Somatic sensation from the pericardium travels in somatic afferent fibers of the phrenic nerve, and referred pain may be felt in the supraclavicular shoulder/neck dermatomes C3-C5.

rationales.a: Deep cardiac plexus carries autonomic cardiac fibers, not the referred somatic pericardial pain pathway.
rationales.b: Superficial cardiac plexus is likewise autonomic rather than the somatic afferent route.
rationales.d: Subcostal nerve serves the lower abdominal wall and is unrelated to pericardial referral.

marrow__ANAT_CH42_Q009.takeaway: The phrenic nerve passes anterior to the lung hilum; tumor there can injure it and elevate/paralyze the ipsilateral diaphragm.
marrow__ANAT_CH42_Q009.displayText: The right phrenic nerve is most likely involved because it passes anterior to the lung hilum. The phrenic nerve provides the sole motor supply to the diaphragm; paralysis causes the respective dome to flatten when intact or move paradoxically on inspiration. The source contrasts the vagus nerve, which passes posterior to the hilum, and notes that recurrent laryngeal nerves are not related to the lung surface in this way.

rationales.c: Vagus nerve passes posterior to the hilum, opposite the described anterior tumor relationship.

marrow__ANAT_CH42_Q011.takeaway: In the neck the phrenic nerve descends on the anterior surface of scalenus anterior before entering the thorax.
marrow__ANAT_CH42_Q011.displayText: The source identifies left phrenic palsy from paradoxical elevation of the left dome and states that the left phrenic nerve runs anterior to scalenus anterior. In the cervical region both phrenic nerves pass anterior to scalenus anterior and posterior to sternocleidomastoid/inferior belly of omohyoid. The left phrenic nerve is posterior to internal jugular vein, transverse cervical artery and suprascapular artery, and posterior to the thoracic duct on the left. At the root of the neck it runs medial to the brachial plexus, anterior to the second part of the subclavian artery and posterior to the subclavian vein. In the thorax it descends anterior to the pulmonary hilum.

marrow__ANAT_CH42_Q012.takeaway: The superior intercostal artery branches from the costocervical trunk and supplies the first two posterior intercostal spaces.
marrow__ANAT_CH42_Q012.displayText: The superior intercostal artery is a branch of the costocervical trunk. It descends in front of the necks of the first two ribs and gives rise to the first two posterior intercostal arteries. The source notes that it is not constant and is more common on the right; when absent it is replaced by a direct branch from the aorta.

marrow__ANAT_CH42_Q013.takeaway: Each of the upper nine intercostal spaces has two anterior intercostal arteries; spaces 10–11 have none.
marrow__ANAT_CH42_Q013.displayText: Each of the upper nine intercostal spaces has two anterior intercostal arteries and one posterior intercostal artery. The 10th and 11th intercostal spaces have no anterior intercostal artery. The source states that anterior intercostal arteries arise from the internal thoracic artery in the upper six spaces and from the musculophrenic artery in the seventh to ninth spaces, and they anastomose with the corresponding posterior intercostal arteries and their collaterals.

rationales.d: They anastomose with posterior intercostal arteries; the direct source description is not simply anastomosis with internal thoracic artery.

marrow__ANAT_CH42_Q014.takeaway: Posterior intercostal arteries arise from the aorta/superior intercostal trunk, not internal thoracic artery, so they are the exception after internal thoracic injury.
marrow__ANAT_CH42_Q014.displayText: Posterior intercostal arteries are not branches of the internal thoracic artery, so their flow is not directly reduced by injury to it. The source lists branches of the internal thoracic artery including terminal branches at the level of the sixth intercostal space (superior epigastric and musculophrenic), sternal branches, anterior intercostal arteries for the first six spaces, and perforating branches that pierce and supply pectoralis major before becoming cutaneous vessels.
